title: Product of Array Except Self
description: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i] without using division.
constraints: Edge Cases: Array containing one zero (all outputs zero except at zero's index), multiple zeros (all outputs zero).

editorial.step1: Input: nums: list[int]. Output: list[int]. Constraints: 2 <= len(nums) <= 10^5, -30 <= nums[i] <= 30. Edge Cases: Array containing one zero (all outputs zero except at zero's index), multiple zeros (all outputs zero).
editorial.step2: For each element i, compute product of all j != i. Time O(n^2), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Prefix and Suffix Products: Make answer[i] store product of all elements to the left. Then sweep right-to-left with a running suffix product variable.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) two linear passes. Space O(1) auxiliary space (output array does not count towards extra space).
editorial.solutionCode:
def productExceptSelf(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    res = [1] * n
    # Prefix pass: res[i] contains product of all elements to the left of i
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):
        res[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    # Suffix pass: multiply with accumulated product of elements to the right of i
    postfix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        res[i] *= postfix
        postfix *= nums[i]
    return res

title: Valid Sudoku
description: Determine if a 9x9 Sudoku board is valid according to standard rules without solving it.
constraints: Edge Cases: Board with only '.' (valid), duplicate in same 3x3 box but different row/col.

editorial.step1: Input: board: list[list[str]] of size 9x9 with digits '1'-'9' and '.'. Output: bool. Constraints: Exactly 9x9 grid. Edge Cases: Board with only '.' (valid), duplicate in same 3x3 box but different row/col.
editorial.step2: Scan each row, each column, and each 3x3 box independently using 3 separate passes. Time O(1), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Single pass using 9 row sets, 9 column sets, and 9 box sets (indexed by (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3). Check for presence before adding.
editorial.step5: Time O(1) constant 81 cells examined. Space O(1) fixed set storage of at most 81 elements.
editorial.solutionCode:
def isValidSudoku(board: list[list[str]]) -> bool:
    rows = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    cols = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    boxes = [set() for _ in range(9)]  # 3x3 sub-grids indexed 0 to 8

    for r in range(9):
        for c in range(9):
            val = board[r][c]
            if val == '.':
                continue
            box_idx = (r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3)
            # Check for duplicate in row, column, or 3x3 block
            if val in rows[r] or val in cols[c] or val in boxes[box_idx]:
                return False
            rows[r].add(val)
            cols[c].add(val)
            boxes[box_idx].add(val)
    return True

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence in O(n) time.
constraints: Edge Cases: Empty array returns 0. Duplicate values.

editorial.step1: Input: nums: list[int]. Output: int. Constraints: 0 <= len(nums) <= 10^5, -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9. Edge Cases: Empty array returns 0. Duplicate values.
editorial.step2: Sort the array and count longest contiguous run of consecutive values. Time O(n log n), Space O(n).
editorial.step3: Convert nums to a hash set. Only start counting sequence length from x if x - 1 is NOT in the set (ensuring we only traverse each sequence from its true start).
editorial.step5: Time O(n) because each number is visited at most twice (once in outer loop, once in inner while loop). Space O(n) for the hash set.
editorial.solutionCode:
def longestConsecutive(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    num_set = set(nums)
    longest = 0
    for x in num_set:
        # Only start counting if x is the true beginning of a streak
        if x - 1 not in num_set:
            curr = x
            streak = 1
            # Expand consecutive streak upwards
            while curr + 1 in num_set:
                curr += 1
                streak += 1
            longest = max(longest, streak)
    return longest

title: Container With Most Water
description: Given an integer array height of length n, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container that contains the most water.
constraints: Edge Cases: All equal heights, decreasing heights.

editorial.step1: Input: height: list[int]. Output: int (max area). Constraints: 2 <= len(height) <= 10^5. Edge Cases: All equal heights, decreasing heights.
editorial.step2: Check area for all pairs (i, j). Time O(n^2), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Two pointers at boundaries l=0, r=n-1. Area is (r - l) * min(h[l], h[r]). Greedily advance the pointer with the smaller height, as moving the taller one cannot increase area.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) single pass converging pointers. Space O(1) constant memory.
editorial.solutionCode:
def maxArea(height: list[int]) -> int:
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    max_water = 0
    while l < r:
        width = r - l
        # Volume bounded by the shorter line
        h = min(height[l], height[r])
        max_water = max(max_water, width * h)
        # Greedily discard the shorter wall (it cannot support larger area)
        if height[l] < height[r]:
            l += 1
        else:
            r -= 1
    return max_water

title: Trapping Rain Water
description: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
constraints: Edge Cases: Less than 3 bars, strictly ascending/descending bars trap 0 water.

editorial.step1: Input: height: list[int]. Output: int. Constraints: 1 <= len(height) <= 2 * 10^4. Edge Cases: Less than 3 bars, strictly ascending/descending bars trap 0 water.
editorial.step2: For each bar i, find max left and max right height: water[i] = max(0, min(max_L, max_R) - h[i]). Time O(n^2), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Two pointers l=0, r=n-1 with left_max, right_max. If left_max < right_max, water trapped at l is governed by left_max, so add left_max - height[l] and l+=1; else process r.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) single pass. Space O(1) auxiliary pointers.
editorial.solutionCode:
def trap(height: list[int]) -> int:
    if not height:
        return 0
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    max_l, max_r = height[l], height[r]
    water = 0
    while l < r:
        # Water level is always constrained by the smaller boundary maximum
        if max_l <= max_r:
            l += 1
            max_l = max(max_l, height[l])
            water += max_l - height[l]  # Trapped water above bar l
        else:
            r -= 1
            max_r = max(max_r, height[r])
            water += max_r - height[r]  # Trapped water above bar r
    return water

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
description: Given a string s and an integer k, you can choose up to k characters and replace them with any uppercase English letter. Return length of longest substring containing the same letter.
constraints: Edge Cases: k >= len(s) returns len(s).

editorial.step1: Input: s: str, k: int. Output: int. Constraints: 1 <= len(s) <= 10^5, uppercase English letters, 0 <= k <= len(s). Edge Cases: k >= len(s) returns len(s).
editorial.step2: Check all substrings, count max freq char, check if window_len - max_freq <= k. Time O(n^2), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Sliding window [l, r] with frequency map and max_freq. A window is valid if (r - l + 1) - max_freq <= k. If invalid, shrink from left l += 1.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) each character visited twice. Space O(26) = O(1) for uppercase English letters.
editorial.solutionCode:
from collections import defaultdict

def characterReplacement(s: str, k: int) -> int:
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    max_freq = 0  # Frequency of most frequent character in current window
    l = 0
    max_len = 0
    for r in range(len(s)):
        counts[s[r]] += 1
        max_freq = max(max_freq, counts[s[r]])
        # If required replacements (window_len - max_freq) exceeds k, shrink window
        while (r - l + 1) - max_freq > k:
            counts[s[l]] -= 1
            l += 1
        max_len = max(max_len, r - l + 1)
    return max_len

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Given an array of integers nums, there is a sliding window of size k moving from left to right. Return the max sliding window.

editorial.step1: Input: nums: list[int], k: int. Output: list[int]. Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 10^5, 1 <= k <= len(nums). Edge Cases: k = 1 returns nums.
editorial.step2: Find max of every subarray of length k. Time O(n * k), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Monotonic Decreasing Deque storing indices: elements in deque are in decreasing order of value. Pop from right elements smaller than current; pop from left elements outside window.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) as each element is pushed and popped at most once. Space O(k) for the deque.
editorial.solutionCode:
from collections import deque

def maxSlidingWindow(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    # Monotonic queue storing indices; elements are kept in strictly decreasing order
    q = deque()
    res = []
    for r in range(len(nums)):
        # Maintain monotonic property: pop smaller elements from the back
        while q and nums[q[-1]] < nums[r]:
            q.pop()
        q.append(r)
        # Evict elements that fell outside the sliding window boundary
        if q[0] < r - k + 1:
            q.popleft()
        # Record maximum (head of deque) once first window is formed
        if r >= k - 1:
            res.append(nums[q[0]])
    return res

title: Generate Parentheses
description: Given n pairs of parentheses, write a function to generate all combinations of well-formed parentheses.

editorial.step1: Input: n: int. Output: list[str]. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 8. Edge Cases: n=1 returns ['()'].
editorial.step2: Generate all 2^(2n) sequences of '(' and ')' and validate each. Time O(2^(2n) * n), Space O(n).
editorial.step3: Backtracking with pruning: add '(' if open_count < n; add ')' if close_count < open_count. Base case: len == 2n.
editorial.step5: Time O(4^n / sqrt(n)) bounded by the nth Catalan number. Space O(n) recursion call stack depth.
editorial.solutionCode:
def generateParenthesis(n: int) -> list[str]:
    res = []
    stack = []

    def backtrack(open_c: int, close_c: int) -> None:
        # Base case: valid string of length 2n constructed
        if open_c == close_c == n:
            res.append("".join(stack))
            return
        # Choice 1: Add opening parenthesis if budget remains
        if open_c < n:
            stack.append("(")
            backtrack(open_c + 1, close_c)
            stack.pop()
        # Choice 2: Add closing parenthesis only if it doesn't exceed open brackets
        if close_c < open_c:
            stack.append(")")
            backtrack(open_c, close_c + 1)
            stack.pop()

    backtrack(0, 0)
    return res

description: Given an array of integers temperatures represents the daily temperatures, return an array answer such that answer[i] is the number of days you have to wait after the ith day to get a warmer temperature.
constraints: Edge Cases: No warmer day in future gives 0.

editorial.step1: Input: temperatures: list[int]. Output: list[int]. Constraints: 1 <= len(temperatures) <= 10^5. Edge Cases: No warmer day in future gives 0.
editorial.step2: For each day i, scan forward j > i until temperatures[j] > temperatures[i]. Time O(n^2), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Monotonic Decreasing Stack of indices: for each day i, pop indices prev where T[prev] < T[i], setting res[prev] = i - prev.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) each index is pushed and popped at most once. Space O(n) for monotonic stack.
editorial.solutionCode:
def dailyTemperatures(temperatures: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(temperatures)
    res = [0] * n
    # Monotonic decreasing stack storing indices: [index]
    stack = []
    for i, t in enumerate(temperatures):
        # Resolve wait time for all previous days colder than today
        while stack and temperatures[stack[-1]] < t:
            prev_idx = stack.pop()
            res[prev_idx] = i - prev_idx
        stack.append(i)
    return res

editorial.step1: Input: heights: list[int]. Output: int. Constraints: 1 <= len(heights) <= 10^5. Edge Cases: All bars equal height, strictly increasing/decreasing.
editorial.step2: For every bar i, expand left and right as long as adjacent bars >= heights[i]. Time O(n^2), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Monotonic Increasing Stack storing (index, height). When popping a taller bar h, its right boundary is current index i, and left boundary is the start index it extended back to.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) single pass with monotonic stack. Space O(n) for stack.
editorial.solutionCode:
def largestRectangleArea(heights: list[int]) -> int:
    max_area = 0
    # Monotonic increasing stack storing pairs of (start_index, height)
    stack = []
    for i, h in enumerate(heights):
        start = i
        # Pop bars taller than current bar and calculate their maximum rectangle
        while stack and stack[-1][1] > h:
            prev_idx, prev_h = stack.pop()
            max_area = max(max_area, prev_h * (i - prev_idx))
            start = prev_idx  # Current bar can extend back to popped bar's start
        stack.append((start, h))
    
    # Process remaining bars in stack that extend to the rightmost boundary
    n = len(heights)
    for idx, h in stack:
        max_area = max(max_area, h * (n - idx))
    return max_area

description: Koko loves to eat bananas. There are n piles of bananas. Return the minimum integer k such that she can eat all the bananas within h hours.
constraints: Edge Cases: h == len(piles) requires k = max(piles).

editorial.step1: Input: piles: list[int], h: int. Output: int. Constraints: len(piles) <= h <= 10^9, 1 <= piles[i] <= 10^9. Edge Cases: h == len(piles) requires k = max(piles).

editorial.step5: Time O(n * log(max(piles))) where n is number of piles. Space O(1) constant memory.
editorial.solutionCode:
import math

def minEatingSpeed(piles: list[int], h: int) -> int:
    # Binary search on eating speed k: range [1, max(piles)]
    l, r = 1, max(piles)
    res = r
    while l <= r:
        k = l + (r - l) // 2
        # Calculate total hours needed at speed k
        total_hours = sum(math.ceil(pile / k) for pile in piles)
        if total_hours <= h:
            res = k      # Valid speed, try to find a slower viable speed
            r = k - 1
        else:
            l = k + 1    # Too slow, need to eat faster
    return res

def mergeTwoLists(list1: ListNode | None, list2: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
    # Dummy head simplifies edge cases when appending first node
    dummy = ListNode()
    tail = dummy
    while list1 and list2:
        if list1.val <= list2.val:
            tail.next = list1
            list1 = list1.next
        else:
            tail.next = list2
            list2 = list2.next
        tail = tail.next

    tail.next = list1 if list1 else list2
    return dummy.next

editorial.solutionCode:
def reorderList(head: ListNode | None) -> None:
    if not head or not head.next:
        return
    # 1. Split list in half using fast & slow pointers
    slow, fast = head, head.next
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    second = slow.next
    slow.next = None  # Sever first half from second half

    # 2. Reverse the second half
    prev = None
    curr = second
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    second = prev

    # 3. Interleave nodes from first and second halves
    first = head
    while second:
        tmp1, tmp2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = tmp1
        first, second = tmp1, tmp2

def removeNthFromEnd(head: ListNode | None, n: int) -> ListNode | None:
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    left = dummy
    right = head
    # Advance right pointer n steps forward
    for _ in range(n):
        right = right.next
    # Move both pointers until right reaches past the tail
    while right:
        left = left.next
        right = right.next
    # Left is now positioned directly before the target node to delete
    left.next = left.next.next
    return dummy.next

def addTwoNumbers(l1: ListNode | None, l2: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
    dummy = ListNode()
    curr = dummy
    carry = 0

        v2 = l2.val if l2 else 0

def findDuplicate(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    # Cycle detection treating value as next pointer: index -> nums[index]
    slow = fast = 0
    # Phase 1: Locate meeting point inside the cycle
    while True:
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[nums[fast]]
        if slow == fast:
            break
    # Phase 2: Find cycle entrance by resetting slow pointer to start
    slow2 = 0
    while slow != slow2:
        slow = nums[slow]
        slow2 = nums[slow2]
    return slow

title: LRU Cache
description: Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache with get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1) time.

editorial.step1: Output: Class LRUCache(capacity) with get and put. Constraints: 1 <= capacity <= 3000, all operations O(1) average time.
editorial.step2: List of (key, value) with linear search on get/put. Time O(capacity) per op, Space O(capacity).
editorial.step3: Hash Map + Doubly Linked List with dummy head and tail. Hash map maps key -> DListNode for O(1) lookup. Doubly linked list allows O(1) node removal and insertion to MRU front.
editorial.step5: Time O(1) strictly for get() and put(). Space O(capacity) for hash map and doubly linked nodes.
editorial.solutionCode:
class DNode:
    def __init__(self, key=0, val=0):
        self.key = key
        self.val = val
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.cache = {}  # key -> DNode
        # Sentinel dummy nodes eliminate edge checks on empty list
        self.head, self.tail = DNode(), DNode()
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def _remove(self, node: DNode) -> None:
        # Unlink node from its current position
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def _add_to_front(self, node: DNode) -> None:
        # Splice node immediately after dummy head (most recently used)
        node.next = self.head.next
        node.prev = self.head
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        if key in self.cache:
            node = self.cache[key]
            self._remove(node)
            self._add_to_front(node)  # Refresh recency
            return node.val
        return -1

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        if key in self.cache:
            node = self.cache[key]
            node.val = value
            self._remove(node)
            self._add_to_front(node)
        else:
            # If capacity exceeded, evict least recently used (before tail)
            if len(self.cache) >= self.cap:
                lru = self.tail.prev
                self._remove(lru)
                del self.cache[lru.key]
            new_node = DNode(key, value)
            self._add_to_front(new_node)
            self.cache[key] = new_node

import heapq

def mergeKLists(lists: list[ListNode | None]) -> ListNode | None:
    # Min-heap storing tuples: (node_value, list_index, node)
    heap = []
    for i, node in enumerate(lists):
        if node:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.val, i, node))
            
    dummy = ListNode()
    curr = dummy
    while heap:
        val, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        curr.next = node
        curr = curr.next
        # Advance the extracted list and reinsert next node into heap
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
description: Given the head of a linked list, reverse the nodes of the list k at a time, and return the modified list. Nodes left over at the end should remain as-is.
constraints: Edge Cases: k = 1 (no-op), length < k (no change).

editorial.step1: Input: head: Optional[ListNode], k: int. Output: Optional[ListNode]. Constraints: 1 <= k <= sz <= 5000. Edge Cases: k = 1 (no-op), length < k (no change).
editorial.step2: Extract nodes to list in groups of k, reverse slices, and rebuild. Time O(n), Space O(n).
editorial.step3: Group-by-group in-place reversal: check if k nodes exist ahead. If so, reverse those k nodes, reconnect with previous group tail and next group head.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) single pass over nodes. Space O(1) in-place pointer updates.
editorial.solutionCode:
def reverseKGroup(head: ListNode | None, k: int) -> ListNode | None:
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    group_prev = dummy

    def get_kth(curr: ListNode | None, k: int) -> ListNode | None:
        while curr and k > 0:
            curr = curr.next
            k -= 1
        return curr

    while True:
        kth = get_kth(group_prev, k)
        # If fewer than k nodes remain, leave them untouched
        if not kth:
            break
        group_next = kth.next

        # Reverse nodes between group_prev and group_next
        prev, curr = kth.next, group_prev.next
        while curr != group_next:
            nxt = curr.next
            curr.next = prev
            prev = curr
            curr = nxt

        # Connect previous group tail to newly reversed group head
        tmp = group_prev.next
        group_prev.next = kth
        group_prev = tmp
    return dummy.next

editorial.solutionCode:
def diameterOfBinaryTree(root: TreeNode | None) -> int:
    max_d = 0

    def height(node: TreeNode | None) -> int:
        nonlocal max_d
        if not node:
            return 0
        left_h = height(node.left)
        right_h = height(node.right)
        # Longest path through this node is sum of left and right branch heights
        max_d = max(max_d, left_h + right_h)
        # Return height of subtree to parent
        return 1 + max(left_h, right_h)

    height(root)
    return max_d

editorial.solutionCode:
def kthSmallest(root: TreeNode | None, k: int) -> int:
    # In-order traversal of BST visits nodes in strictly increasing order
    stack = []
    curr = root
    while curr or stack:
        # Traverse down left spine
        while curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return curr.val
        curr = curr.right
    return -1

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
description: Given two integer arrays preorder and inorder where preorder is the preorder traversal of a binary tree and inorder is the inorder traversal of the same tree, construct and return the binary tree.

editorial.step1: Input: preorder: list[int], inorder: list[int]. Output: Optional[TreeNode]. Constraints: 1 <= len <= 3000, unique values. Edge Cases: Single node.
editorial.step2: Linear search for root in inorder on each recursion step. Time O(n^2), Space O(n).

editorial.step5: Time O(n) builds n nodes with O(1) hash map lookups. Space O(n) for in_map and recursion stack.
editorial.solutionCode:
def buildTree(preorder: list[int], inorder: list[int]) -> TreeNode | None:
    # Preorder: [Root, Left Subtree, Right Subtree]
    # Inorder:  [Left Subtree, Root, Right Subtree]
    in_map = {val: idx for idx, val in enumerate(inorder)}
    pre_idx = 0

    def helper(l: int, r: int) -> TreeNode | None:
        nonlocal pre_idx
        if l > r:
            return None
        # Root value is determined by next element in preorder traversal
        root_val = preorder[pre_idx]
        pre_idx += 1
        root = TreeNode(root_val)
        mid = in_map[root_val]

        # Construct left subtree before right subtree to match preorder sequence
        root.left = helper(l, mid - 1)
        root.right = helper(mid + 1, r)
        return root

    return helper(0, len(inorder) - 1)

title: Last Stone Weight
description: You are given an array of integers stones. Smash the two heaviest stones x and y (x <= y): if x == y both destroyed, if x != y new stone has weight y - x. Return weight of last stone or 0.

editorial.step1: Input: stones: list[int]. Output: int. Constraints: 1 <= len(stones) <= 30.
editorial.step2: Sort on each smash. Time O(n^2 log n), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Max-Heap (simulated via inverted negatives with min-heap): pop two largest y and x. If y > x, push -(y - x).
editorial.step5: Time O(n log n) heap operations. Space O(n) heap memory.
editorial.solutionCode:
import heapq

def lastStoneWeight(stones: list[int]) -> int:
    # Invert signs to simulate a max-heap using Python heapq
    max_heap = [-s for s in stones]
    heapq.heapify(max_heap)

    while len(max_heap) > 1:
        s1 = -heapq.heappop(max_heap)
        s2 = -heapq.heappop(max_heap)
        # If stones have different weights, smash and push difference back
        if s1 != s2:
            heapq.heappush(max_heap, -(s1 - s2))
    return -max_heap[0] if max_heap else 0

import heapq

def kClosest(points: list[list[int]], k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
    # Max-heap of size k storing: (-dist_squared, x, y)
    max_heap = []
    for x, y in points:
        dist = x * x + y * y
        heapq.heappush(max_heap, (-dist, x, y))
        # Keep heap bounded to k points; furthest point evicted at root
        if len(max_heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(max_heap)
    return [[x, y] for _, x, y in max_heap]

title: Task Scheduler
description: Given a characters array tasks and non-negative integer n (cooling interval), return least number of intervals to execute all tasks.

editorial.step1: Input: tasks: list[str], n: int. Output: int. Constraints: 1 <= len(tasks) <= 10^4, 0 <= n <= 100.
editorial.step2: Simulate round-robin scheduling with a priority queue. Time O(time * log 26), Space O(26).

editorial.step5: Time O(len(tasks)) single pass counting. Space O(26) = O(1) character frequency map.
editorial.solutionCode:
from collections import Counter, deque
import heapq

def leastInterval(tasks: list[str], n: int) -> int:
    counts = Counter(tasks)
    # Max-heap tracking task frequencies
    max_heap = [-cnt for cnt in counts.values()]
    heapq.heapify(max_heap)
    
    time = 0
    # Cooldown queue storing pairs: [remaining_count, available_time]
    q = deque()
    while max_heap or q:
        time += 1
        if max_heap:
            cnt = 1 + heapq.heappop(max_heap)
            if cnt != 0:
                q.append([cnt, time + n])
        # Re-queue task once cooling interval n has elapsed
        if q and q[0][1] == time:
            heapq.heappush(max_heap, q.popleft()[0])
    return time

title: Subsets
description: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set).

editorial.step5: Time O(n * 2^n) total states and copying. Space O(n) recursion call stack depth.
editorial.solutionCode:
def subsets(nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    res = []
    subset = []

    def dfs(i: int) -> None:
        # Base case: reached beyond array end, record subset copy
        if i >= len(nums):
            res.append(subset.copy())
            return
        # Decision 1: Include nums[i]
        subset.append(nums[i])
        dfs(i + 1)
        # Decision 2: Exclude nums[i] (backtrack)
        subset.pop()
        dfs(i + 1)

    dfs(0)
    return res

description: Given an array of distinct integers candidates and a target integer target, return a list of all unique combinations where the chosen numbers sum to target (numbers can be reused unlimited times).

editorial.step2: Exhaustive recursive search with set. Time O(2^target), Space O(target).
editorial.step3: Backtracking with reuse: at index i, branch 1 includes candidates[i] and stays at i (reducing target); branch 2 advances to i + 1.
editorial.step5: Time O(2^(target/min_val)) bounded by recursion tree. Space O(target/min_val) recursion depth.
editorial.solutionCode:
def combinationSum(candidates: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
    res = []

    def dfs(i: int, curr: list[int], total: int) -> None:
        if total == target:
            res.append(curr.copy())
            return
        if i >= len(candidates) or total > target:
            return
        # Branch 1: Pick candidate[i] (can be reused indefinitely)
        curr.append(candidates[i])
        dfs(i, curr, total + candidates[i])
        # Branch 2: Skip candidate[i] and move to next candidate
        curr.pop()
        dfs(i + 1, curr, total)

    dfs(0, [], 0)
    return res

def subsetsWithDup(nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    nums.sort()  # Sort to bring duplicate elements adjacent
    res = []
    subset = []

    def dfs(i: int) -> None:
        if i >= len(nums):
            res.append(subset.copy())
            return
        # Decision 1: Include nums[i]
        subset.append(nums[i])
        dfs(i + 1)
        subset.pop()
        # Decision 2: Exclude nums[i] and skip all identical duplicates
        while i + 1 < len(nums) and nums[i] == nums[i + 1]:
            i += 1
        dfs(i + 1)

    dfs(0)
    return res

editorial.step5: Time O(n!) search space with diagonal pruning. Space O(n^2) for board and recursion sets.
editorial.solutionCode:
def solveNQueens(n: int) -> list[list[str]]:
    col_set = set()
    pos_diag = set()  # (r + c)
    neg_diag = set()  # (r - c)
    res = []
    board = [["."] * n for _ in range(n)]

    def backtrack(r: int) -> None:
        if r == n:
            res.append(["".join(row) for row in board])
            return
        for c in range(n):
            if c in col_set or (r + c) in pos_diag or (r - c) in neg_diag:
                continue
            # Place Queen
            col_set.add(c)
            pos_diag.add(r + c)
            neg_diag.add(r - c)
            board[r][c] = "Q"

            backtrack(r + 1)

            # Remove Queen (backtrack)
            col_set.remove(c)
            pos_diag.remove(r + c)
            neg_diag.remove(r - c)
            board[r][c] = "."

    backtrack(0)
    return res

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
description: Given an m x n matrix of heights, find all grid coordinates where water can flow to both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.

editorial.step1: Input: heights: list[list[int]]. Output: list[list[int]]. Constraints: 1 <= m, n <= 200.
editorial.step2: Simulate flow from every cell individually. Time O((m * n)^2), Space O(m * n).

editorial.step5: Time O(m * n) two BFS/DFS passes. Space O(m * n) for reachability sets.
editorial.solutionCode:
def pacificAtlantic(heights: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
    ROWS, COLS = len(heights), len(heights[0])
    pac, atl = set(), set()

    def dfs(r: int, c: int, visit: set, prev_h: int) -> None:
        if ((r, c) in visit or not (0 <= r < ROWS and 0 <= c < COLS)
                or heights[r][c] < prev_h):
            return
        visit.add((r, c))
        # Flow water uphill into adjacent interior cells
        dfs(r + 1, c, visit, heights[r][c])
        dfs(r - 1, c, visit, heights[r][c])
        dfs(r, c + 1, visit, heights[r][c])
        dfs(r, c - 1, visit, heights[r][c])

    # Seed searches from coastal boundary edges
    for c in range(COLS):
        dfs(0, c, pac, heights[0][c])
        dfs(ROWS - 1, c, atl, heights[ROWS - 1][c])
    for r in range(ROWS):
        dfs(r, 0, pac, heights[r][0])
        dfs(r, COLS - 1, atl, heights[r][COLS - 1])

    # Intersect cells that can reach both oceans
    return list(pac & atl)

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
description: Given a list of airline tickets where tickets[i] = [fromi, toi], reconstruct the itinerary in order and return it starting from 'JFK' using all tickets with smallest lexical order.

editorial.step1: Input: tickets: list[list[str]]. Output: list[str]. Constraints: 1 <= len(tickets) <= 300.
editorial.step2: Backtracking exploring all permutations of tickets. Time O(E!), Space O(E).
editorial.step3: Hierholzer's Algorithm (Eulerian Path / Post-order DFS): sort outgoing edges in reverse lexical order. Run DFS popping edges; append airport to itinerary on post-order exit, then reverse.
editorial.step5: Time O(E log E) sorting edges + O(E) Hierholzer traversal. Space O(V + E) for adjacency list.
editorial.solutionCode:
from collections import defaultdict

def findItinerary(tickets: list[list[str]]) -> list[str]:
    # Hierholzer's Algorithm for Eulerian Path
    adj = defaultdict(list)
    # Sort destinations in reverse lexical order so we can pop from the back in O(1)
    for src, dst in sorted(tickets, reverse=True):
        adj[src].append(dst)

    res = []
    def dfs(airport: str):
        while adj[airport]:
            next_dest = adj[airport].pop()
            dfs(next_dest)
        res.append(airport)

    dfs("JFK")
    return res[::-1]

description: Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s.

editorial.step5: Time O(n^2) 2n expansions of at most n steps. Space O(1) in-place indices.
editorial.solutionCode:
def longestPalindrome(s: str) -> str:
    res = ""
    res_len = 0

    def expand(l: int, r: int) -> None:
        nonlocal res, res_len
        # Expand outwards from center while characters match
        while l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]:
            if (r - l + 1) > res_len:
                res = s[l : r + 1]
                res_len = r - l + 1
            l -= 1
            r += 1

    for i in range(len(s)):
        # Odd-length palindromes (single-character center)
        expand(i, i)
        # Even-length palindromes (two-character center)
        expand(i, i + 1)
    return res

def countSubstrings(s: str) -> int:
    count = 0

    def count_pal(l: int, r: int) -> int:
        c = 0
        while l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]:
            c += 1
            l -= 1
            r += 1
        return c

        count += count_pal(i, i)
        count += count_pal(i, i + 1)
    return count

def numDecodings(s: str) -> int:
    # If string starts with '0', no valid decoding exists
    if not s or s[0] == "0":
        return 0
    # dp1 = ways to decode up to i-1, dp2 = ways up to i-2
    dp1, dp2 = 1, 1
    for i in range(1, len(s)):
        curr = 0
        # Single-digit decode ('1' to '9')
        if s[i] != "0":
            curr += dp1
        # Two-digit decode ('10' to '26')
        two_digit = int(s[i - 1 : i + 1])
        if 10 <= two_digit <= 26:
            curr += dp2
        dp2 = dp1
        dp1 = curr
    return dp1

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
description: You are given an array prices. You may complete as many transactions as you like, but after you sell your stock, you cannot buy stock on the next day (cooldown of 1 day). Return max profit.

editorial.step1: Input: prices: list[int]. Output: int. Constraints: 1 <= len(prices) <= 5000.
editorial.step2: DFS with memoization (i, buying state). Time O(n), Space O(n).
editorial.step3: State Machine DP: maintain 3 states at day i: `held` (holding stock), `sold` (just sold stock, in cooldown tomorrow), `rest` (holding no stock, can buy).
editorial.step5: Time O(n) single pass. Space O(1) state variables.
editorial.solutionCode:
def maxProfit(prices: list[int]) -> int:
    # Finite State Machine:
    # held: currently holding a stock
    # sold: sold stock today (forces mandatory 1-day cooldown)
    # rest: ready to buy
    held = float('-inf')
    sold = 0
    rest = 0

    for p in prices:
        prev_sold = sold
        sold = held + p             # Sell held stock
        held = max(held, rest - p)  # Buy new stock from rest state
        rest = max(rest, prev_sold) # Rest or recover from cooldown
    return max(sold, rest)

title: Target Sum

editorial.step1: Input: nums: list[int], target: int. Output: int. Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 20, sum(nums) <= 1000.

editorial.step3: Mathematical reduction to Subset Sum: let P be positive subset, N negative subset. P - N = target and P + N = total -> 2P = target + total -> P = (target + total) / 2.
editorial.step5: Time O(n * subset_sum). Space O(subset_sum) 1D DP array.
editorial.solutionCode:
from collections import defaultdict

def findTargetSumWays(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    # dp maps sum -> number of ways to achieve it
    dp = defaultdict(int)
    dp[0] = 1

    for n in nums:
        next_dp = defaultdict(int)
        for cur_sum, count in dp.items():
            next_dp[cur_sum + n] += count
            next_dp[cur_sum - n] += count
        dp = next_dp
    return dp[target]

editorial.solutionCode:
def maxSubArray(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    # Kadane's Algorithm
    max_sum = nums[0]
    cur_sum = 0
    for x in nums:
        # Reset current sum if prefix contribution drops below 0
        cur_sum = max(x, cur_sum + x)
        max_sum = max(max_sum, cur_sum)
    return max_sum

title: Jump Game II
description: Given an array of non-negative integers nums, return the minimum number of jumps to reach nums[n - 1].

editorial.step1: Input: nums: list[int]. Output: int. Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 10^4.
editorial.step2: BFS on jump graph. Time O(n^2), Space O(n).
editorial.step3: Greedy BFS window [l, r]: in each level (jump), find `farthest = max(i + nums[i] for i in range(l, r+1))`. Then set `l = r + 1` and `r = farthest`.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) each index visited once. Space O(1) constant window boundaries.
editorial.solutionCode:
def jump(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    jumps = 0
    l = r = 0  # Window [l, r] reachable with current number of jumps

    while r < len(nums) - 1:
        farthest = 0
        for i in range(l, r + 1):
            farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
        l = r + 1
        r = farthest
        jumps += 1
    return jumps

editorial.step5: Time O(n log n) sorting and heap pushes. Space O(n) for rooms heap.
editorial.solutionCode:
def minMeetingRooms(intervals: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    # Separate and sort start and end timelines independently
    starts = sorted([i[0] for i in intervals])
    ends = sorted([i[1] for i in intervals])
    res = 0
    count = 0
    s, e = 0, 0

    while s < len(intervals):
        if starts[s] < ends[e]:
            count += 1  # Meeting started before previous ended, need room
            s += 1
        else:
            count -= 1  # Room freed up
            e += 1
        res = max(res, count)
    return res

title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
description: You are given a 2D integer array intervals and queries array. Return an array containing the size of the smallest interval that contains each query point, or -1.

editorial.step1: Input: intervals: list[list[int]], queries: list[int]. Output: list[int]. Constraints: 1 <= len(intervals), len(queries) <= 10^5.
editorial.step2: For each query, scan all intervals to find min length. Time O(Q * N), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Offline Processing + Min-Heap: sort intervals by start time; sort queries with original indices. Sweep queries: push all intervals starting <= q into min-heap of `(length, end)`. Pop intervals with `end < q`. Min length is heap root.
editorial.step5: Time O(N log N + Q log Q) for sorting and heap sweeps. Space O(N + Q) for heap and result.
editorial.solutionCode:
import heapq

def minInterval(intervals: list[list[int]], queries: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    # Min-heap storing: (interval_length, interval_end)
    min_heap = []
    res = {}
    i = 0

    # Sort queries while maintaining original associations
    for q in sorted(queries):
        # Push all intervals starting at or before query q
        while i < len(intervals) and intervals[i][0] <= q:
            l, r = intervals[i]
            heapq.heappush(min_heap, (r - l + 1, r))
            i += 1
        # Evict stale intervals whose end point is before query q
        while min_heap and min_heap[0][1] < q:
            heapq.heappop(min_heap)
        res[q] = min_heap[0][0] if min_heap else -1

    return [res[q] for q in queries]

title: Happy Number
description: Write an algorithm to determine if a number n is happy (repeatedly replace the number by the sum of the squares of its digits until it equals 1, or loops endlessly in a cycle).

editorial.step1: Input: n: int. Output: bool. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2^31 - 1.
editorial.step2: Store seen numbers in a hash set to detect cycles. Time O(log n), Space O(log n).
editorial.step3: Floyd's Fast & Slow Pointers: compute `next_sum(n) = sum(int(d)**2 for d in str(n))`. Advance slow by 1 step, fast by 2 steps until slow == fast or fast == 1.
editorial.step5: Time O(log n) steps to cycle. Space O(1) constant pointers.
editorial.solutionCode:
def isHappy(n: int) -> bool:
    def get_sum(num: int) -> int:
        s = 0
        while num > 0:
            digit = num % 10
            s += digit * digit
            num //= 10
        return s

    # Floyd's Cycle Detection on digit square sums
    slow, fast = n, get_sum(n)
    while fast != 1 and slow != fast:
        slow = get_sum(slow)
        fast = get_sum(get_sum(fast))
    return fast == 1

title: Number of 1 Bits
description: Write a function that takes the binary representation of an unsigned integer and returns the number of '1' bits it has (also known as the Hamming weight).

editorial.step1: Input: n: int. Output: int. Constraints: 32-bit unsigned integer.
editorial.step2: Shift and check 32 times. Time O(32), Space O(1).
editorial.step3: Brian Kernighan's Algorithm: `n &= (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit in O(1). Repeat until n becomes 0.
editorial.step5: Time O(k) where k is number of set bits (at most 32). Space O(1) constant register.
editorial.solutionCode:
def hammingWeight(n: int) -> int:
    count = 0
    while n:
        # Brian Kernighan's Algorithm: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit
        n &= (n - 1)
        count += 1
    return count

title: Reverse Bits
description: Reverse bits of a given 32 bits unsigned integer.
constraints: Input: n: int (32-bit unsigned). Output: int.

editorial.step2: Convert to string of 32 binary digits, reverse, and parse. Time O(32), Space O(32).
editorial.step3: Bitwise Shift: loop 32 times, in each step left-shift result `res = (res << 1) | (n & 1)` and right-shift `n >>= 1`.
editorial.step5: Time O(1) exactly 32 iterations. Space O(1) single integer register.
editorial.solutionCode:
def reverseBits(n: int) -> int:
    res = 0
    for _ in range(32):
        # Shift res left and append least significant bit of n
        res = (res << 1) | (n & 1)
        n >>= 1
    return res

title: Missing Number
description: Given an array nums containing n distinct numbers in the range [0, n], return the only number in the range that is missing from the array.

editorial.step3: XOR Index and Value: `res = n ^ XOR(i ^ nums[i])`. All present numbers cancel with their index, leaving only the missing number.
editorial.step5: Time O(n) single pass. Space O(1) constant register.
editorial.solutionCode:
def missingNumber(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    res = n
    # XOR all array indices and array values; missing number remains
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        res ^= i ^ x
    return res

title: Reverse Integer
description: Given a signed 32-bit integer x, return x with its digits reversed. If reversing x causes the value to go outside [-2^31, 2^31 - 1], return 0.

editorial.step1: Input: x: int. Output: int. Constraints: -2^31 <= x <= 2^31 - 1.
editorial.step2: String conversion with check. Time O(log x), Space O(log x).
editorial.step3: Modulo Arithmetic: pop digit with `digit = x % 10` (handling sign), update `res = res * 10 + digit`. Check 32-bit signed bounds before return.
editorial.step5: Time O(log10(x)) at most 10 digits. Space O(1) constant register.
editorial.solutionCode:
def reverse(x: int) -> int:
    sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1
    x = abs(x)
    res = 0
    # 32-bit signed limits: [-2^31, 2^31 - 1]
    MAX_INT = 2**31 - 1

    while x != 0:
        digit = x % 10
        x //= 10
        # Check for 32-bit overflow before multiplying
        if res > MAX_INT // 10 or (res == MAX_INT // 10 and digit > 7):
            return 0
        res = res * 10 + digit
    return sign * res
